Concept Storyboard — Fabricademy

Multiple paths,
one system.

I wanted to do many things. This is the story of how they turned out to be one thing, seen from different scales.

Scroll ↓

For a long time I thought I had to choose — pattern-making, architecture, public art, textile. Each one felt like its own direction.

Looking back, they were never separate projects. They were the same instinct, tested in four different materials.

PatternArchitecturePublic ArtTextile
01
Childhood / Pattern

Where it started: two gears and a pen.

A Spirograph wasn't a toy for drawing circles — it was a rule that produced endless variation. I filled notebooks with loops I never meant to keep, only to make. This is how my notebooks looked like.

Fig. 01 — Notebook pattern-making, childhood practiceOwn work
02
Architecture / System

Then: a systematic way of seeing.

Studying architecture gave me a different pleasure — designing not a single object, but the system that generates it: units, connections, distribution, structure. Tools and diagrams became a language of their own. This is how my designs looked like.

Fig. 02–03 — Systems diagrams, architectural studio workOwn work
03
Public Art / Scale

In art, I found the scale of the body in public space.

Moving into large-scale public art let the same curved logic step outside the notebook and into a place people could walk around, sit in, pass through. Structure became something shared, not just drawn.

Fig. 04 — Large-scale public art installationOwn work
04
Textile / Touch

Recently: a softer, closer material.

Working with textile came later, almost quietly, as an additional way in. Fabric, rope, and knot let me explore how soft, nostalgic, and sometimes warm a material can be — closer to the body and to memory than anything rigid I'd worked with before.

Fig. 05 — Textile and rope studyOwn work
05
Now

Turning the Spirograph into a 3D system.

The project ahead takes that first childhood curve and gives it volume — the same repeating geometric unit, rebuilt through digital fabrication and textile, carried across five scales instead of staying flat on one page.

"One rule. Five scales. No fixed size."

Scale 01

Wearable

On the body — a modular garment or accessory built from the repeated curve.

Ref. — pattern / network study
Scale 02

Product

As an object — lighting, furniture, or a held piece built from the same module.

Ref. — R. Sweeney, ruled-surface sketch
Scale 03

Façade

At building scale — a porous, structural skin generated by the curve at high density.

Ref. — ruled-surface geometry study
Scale 04

Installation

Indoors — a woven, spatial volume built for a room, not a body.

Ref. — R. Sweeney, curve study
Scale 05

Urban

Outdoors — a canopy or seating element, the pattern grown to city scale.

Ref. — tubular structure precedent
"Four materials, one instinct. The curve I drew at eight years old is still the one I'm building with."
